abstract: When visual information is no longer perceptually available, working memory (WM) allows us to act on sensory representations. But does this guidance require attentional prioritization? We addressed this question by asking participants to remember two oriented bars that were later tested with one predictable and one random probe. This design allowed us to track when a remembered orientation became linked to a specific response hand and whether that link depended on which item was currently prioritized in WM. Response preparation followed prioritization: even when the later response was predictable, no motor preparation emerged while the corresponding item remained latent. Our exploratory analyses showed that prospective action information reduced the need to reprioritize latent items, and that learned stimulus-response mappings generalized across task contexts, suggesting that task-relevant features of visual WM can be partly offloaded onto motor codes. These findings show that active response preparation is coupled with selective attention, while motor representations can also support maintenance in a visual WM task.
